newsitem.title: USA: Top lawmaker, wary of China, urges U.S. think big.
newsitem.headline: Top lawmaker, wary of China, urges U.S. think big.

text.p: The head of the House of Representatives' International Relations Committee has called on President Bill Clinton to draft a charter spelling out plans for preventing China from dominating its neighbours.

Modelled on the 1941 Atlantic Charter in which the United States and Britain laid out a code of conduct, the proposed Pacific Charter should be designed to prevent "regional hegemony by one nation," among other goals, committee chairman Benjamin Gilman said.

In a speech on Wednesday night to a dinner hosted by the Heritage Foundation, a conservative research organisation, Gilman said "perhaps the most significant challenge to peace and prosperity in Asia is the rise of a regional hegemon."

"The People's Republic of China is the most likely candidate in that role," the New York Republican said. "In the absence of a countervailing presence, Asia could well find itself within a Chinese sphere of influence in the not too distant future."

Gilman described his proposal as a comprehensive model for U.S. involvement in the region. He said it should strengthen security arrangments through military base and access agreements, regional security pacts and providing for a U.S. presence following any future Korean reunification.

"It would provide the basis for the continuation of a credible forward presence of U.S. forces to deter aggression, help resolve crises and protect and defend our interests and those of our allies and trading partners," he said.

The policy could also provide for sound long-term relations with China, Gilman said. "The present government in Beijing may have a fundamental misapprehension of U.S. intentions in the Pacific, stemming, in no small measure, from the shifting signals that have been emanating from the Clinton administration."

The Clinton administration has repeatedly rejected any suggestion that it seek to "contain" Communist-ruled China's growing military might, saying it aims instead to build a strong, multi-faceted cooperative relationship.
Gilman said most people agree that China represents the greatest challenge to the United States in the Pacific, "with the potential to be a major destabilising force."
